word_order: SOV — verbs and auxiliary/sentence-final endings consistently appear at clause end (e.g. '가는 목적이 있어가지고', '살았는지는', '먹고 헤어졌는데')
punctuation_present: sometimes — some utterances end with '.', '?' or have internal commas, but many transcribed speech turns have no terminal punctuation at all
register: spontaneous colloquial speech (casual conversational monologue/dialogue, likely transcribed interview or chat)
non_boundary_traps: -요 endings mid-clause used as soft pause not full stop
-거든 used as hedging connector not always sentence-final
repeated fillers like '이제 이제' or '그 그' that look like restarts but are hesitation continuations
trailing '?' after noun phrases used as rhetorical continuation e.g. '호텔카지노?'
target_language_risks: Frequent subject/object pro-drop requires inferring agent from prior context, risking mistranslation if segmented too early
Verb-final structure means the main predicate (and thus sentence meaning/polarity/tense) is only revealed at clause end, so premature segmentation before the verb loses meaning
Sentence-final particles (-거든, -잖아, -네) carry modal/attitude nuance untranslatable in isolation
Topic markers (는/은) often precede long qualifying clauses that must stay attached to their predicate
Frequent self-corrections and fillers can be mistaken for clause boundaries, causing fragmented or garbled English output
notes_for_prompt_writer: This is unedited spontaneous Korean speech with frequent fillers, restarts, and omitted subjects/objects; segmentation should wait for verb-final clause endings (e.g. -는데, -고, -니까, -잖아) rather than punctuation, since punctuation is unreliable. Treat repeated fillers and false starts as non-boundaries, and keep topic-marked NPs attached to their following predicate. Because Korean is strongly head-final, avoid splitting before the main verb/ending, as doing so will strand the sentence's core meaning for the target-language MT step.
